questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client suddenly develops facial droop, left-arm weakness, and slurred speech. What should the RN do first?
choices: Schedule a routine clinic visit next week
Ask the client to sleep and reassess later
Activate the stroke response while assessing ABCs and bedside glucose
Give oral aspirin before imaging
questions.explanation: Sudden focal deficits require immediate stroke activation, airway and circulation assessment, and prompt glucose testing. Treatment choice follows urgent imaging and team evaluation.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A patient is found aphasic at 07:00 after being seen at neurologic baseline at 22:00 the previous night. Which time is last known well?
choices: 22:00, when the patient was last observed at baseline
07:00, when the deficit was discovered
The time the CT scan begins
The time the patient arrives in the emergency department
questions.explanation: Last known well is the last documented or witnessed baseline state, not the discovery or arrival time. The distinction guides imaging and treatment evaluation.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client has sudden vertigo plus double vision, slurred speech, and severe gait ataxia. Which concern should be prioritized?
choices: A benign ear problem has been proven
The patient should walk unassisted to improve balance
Stroke is impossible without facial droop
A posterior-circulation stroke needing urgent evaluation
questions.explanation: A cluster of abrupt brainstem or cerebellar findings can signal posterior-circulation stroke. Missing a typical face-arm pattern does not make the symptoms safe.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Why is urgent brain imaging needed before choosing stroke-specific antithrombotic or reperfusion therapy?
choices: It replaces the neurologic exam entirely
It helps identify hemorrhage and guides the ischemic-versus-hemorrhagic treatment pathway
It proves that every symptom is due to stroke
It permits the RN to choose a thrombolytic without orders
questions.explanation: Symptoms cannot reliably distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke. Emergency imaging is central to excluding bleeding and guiding authorized treatment decisions.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which statement reflects the 2026 AHA/ASA approach to IV thrombolysis for an eligible disabling acute ischemic stroke?
choices: Only alteplase can be considered in the standard window
A low NIHSS always excludes a disabling stroke
Alteplase or tenecteplase may be used in the standard 4.5-hour window after individualized eligibility review
All patients with resolved symptoms should receive IV thrombolysis
questions.explanation: The 2026 guideline supports either alteplase or tenecteplase for eligible disabling deficits within 4.5 hours. Imaging, bleeding risk, and clinical context still determine eligibility.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client with suspected large-vessel occlusion is beyond the usual IV thrombolysis window. Which plan remains important?
choices: Urgent stroke-team review for possible endovascular thrombectomy based on imaging and clinical criteria
Assume no reperfusion option can exist after 4.5 hours
Delay vascular imaging until the next day
Start oral anticoagulation independently
questions.explanation: Selected patients with large-vessel occlusion may benefit from EVT outside the standard IV thrombolysis window. Specialist assessment and appropriate vascular imaging remain time-sensitive.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A stroke patient asks for water before a swallowing screen. What should the RN do?
choices: Offer thin liquids slowly because the patient is awake
Give oral tablets first and screen afterward
Ask the family to test swallowing with food
Keep the patient NPO, including oral medications, until an approved screen is completed
questions.explanation: Dysphagia can occur despite alertness. A validated screen by trained staff should precede food, fluid, or oral medicines to reduce aspiration risk.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: After IV thrombolysis, a client develops a sudden severe headache, vomiting, and worsening weakness. What is the priority response?
choices: Reassure the client that this is expected
Immediately escalate for possible intracranial hemorrhage and follow the stroke emergency protocol
Give food to treat nausea
Wait for the next scheduled neurologic check
questions.explanation: Acute headache, emesis, or neurologic decline after reperfusion may signal intracranial bleeding or another serious complication and requires immediate evaluation.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client's sudden speech difficulty has completely resolved after 20 minutes. Which discharge assumption is unsafe?
choices: A transient event can signal high early stroke risk
The cause may require urgent brain, vessel, and heart evaluation
Resolved symptoms mean no emergency evaluation or prevention plan is needed
New symptoms should prompt emergency services
questions.explanation: TIA symptoms can disappear while risk remains high. Urgent assessment and cause-specific secondary prevention are needed even when the examination returns to baseline.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which statement about secondary stroke prevention is most accurate?
choices: Antithrombotic choice depends on cause; atrial fibrillation often calls for anticoagulation, while noncardioembolic disease commonly uses antiplatelet therapy
Long-term dual antiplatelet therapy is required for every survivor
Atrial fibrillation is irrelevant once speech improves
The RN should stop prescribed medicines whenever the neurologic exam normalizes
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention is etiology-specific. The care team assesses atrial fibrillation, vascular disease, bleeding risk, and other factors before selecting and timing antithrombotic therapy.
